topic: Why short strings play high notes

opening.say: Pluck a guitar string, and you hear a note. Pluck a shorter one, and the note changes. Let's see why.
A string is just a stretched thing that wiggles back and forth, and each full wiggle is called one cycle.
Pitch is how many of those wiggles happen every second. We call that count the frequency, and it's what your ear hears as high or low.

more.say: Think of a child on a swing. A long swing takes a slow, lazy trip, while a short swing zips back and forth quickly.
A string works like that. The wiggle has to travel along its whole length and bounce back, so more length means a longer trip.
A longer trip means fewer wiggles each second. That's a lower frequency, and your ear hears it as a lower pitch.

plan.setup: Watch two strings wiggle side by side.
plan.narration: [[strings-appear]]Here's the picture. A long string and a short one. [[long-wiggle]]The long one has a slow trip to make, so it wiggles slowly. [[short-wiggle]]The short one finishes its trip fast, so it wiggles fast. [[count-cycles]]More wiggles each second means a higher note. [[halve-length]]Cut a string in half, and the frequency doubles.
plan.plan:
strings-appear: two horizontal strings fixed at both ends, one long, one exactly half as long, stacked vertically, labeled L and half of L.
long-wiggle: the long string vibrates in one smooth arc, slowly, about two cycles on screen, so the student sees it is slow.
short-wiggle: the half-length string vibrates in one arc, twice as fast as the long one, clearly quicker.
count-cycles: a counter beside each string shows cycles per second f, the short string's count shown as twice the long one's.
halve-length: the long string is shortened to half; its f label doubles, showing f is inversely proportional to L.
plan.close: What do you think happens to the pitch if you shorten the string to a third?
